opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer starts with not trying to fight them on their own turf. If your plan is to out-pre-train a frontier lab, you've already lost, because that's a capital game and they have orders of magnitude more capital. So the question becomes: where does the leverage actually come from now?

My view is that a lot of it has shifted to the post-training side, to reinforcement learning in particular. Pre-trained models have become remarkably capable base layers, and increasingly you can access strong ones, whether through open weights or partnerships. What turns a smart base model into something that can actually do long-horizon work, like navigating a large codebase, understanding a company's conventions, and shipping a change that holds up, is RL on the right environments with the right reward signals. That's much less about raw compute and much more about taste, data, and how tightly you're coupled to the real problem.

That's where focus becomes an advantage. A big lab is building a general system that has to be good at everything for hundreds of millions of users. That's an incredibly hard product problem, and coding is one of many priorities. If you're a startup and coding agents for real enterprise engineering teams is the only thing you care about, you can go much deeper. You can sit with customers, see where agents break in messy, decades-old codebases, and turn those failures into training signal. That loop between deployment and training is hard for a horizontal player to run with the same intensity.

There's also a product and trust dimension. Enterprises want something that understands their code, their security constraints, and their workflows. Owning that whole stack, from the model's behavior down to the integration, lets you deliver something that feels very different from a general chatbot that happens to write code.

So I'd frame it this way: the labs have the advantage on breadth and base capability. A focused team can have the advantage on depth, on the RL and data flywheel for one domain, and on product. And coding in particular is a domain where rewards are relatively verifiable. Tests pass or fail, code compiles or doesn't, so it's unusually well suited to the kind of RL a smaller, sharp team can push really far. It's not easy, but it's a real path, not just a hope.

r001.rationale: It says a startup focused only on coding can go deeper and gain an advantage in domain-specific depth and product over the labs’ broader systems.

r002.rationale: It describes a tight deployment-and-training feedback loop, but does not clearly say that a startup can make faster progress on its chosen objective.

r003.rationale: It says labs must build general systems and treat coding as one of many priorities, but does not describe effort being spread thinly across multiple evaluations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question we got a lot when we started Reflection, and I think the honest answer is you don't compete on pre-training. That's a game where the scale of capital really matters, and the frontier labs have an enormous structural advantage there. If your plan is to out-pre-train OpenAI or Anthropic or Google, you're going to lose.

But I'd push back a bit on the framing that pre-training is where the value is created. The thing I learned at DeepMind, working on Gemini and before that on reinforcement learning, is that the pre-trained model is really the starting point, not the end point. What actually makes a model good at a task like coding is the post-training, the RL, the environments you build, the reward signals you design. That's the part that turned AlphaGo from a decent imitator of human games into something superhuman. And that part is much less about raw capital and much more about research taste and iteration speed.

So the way I think about it, there's a bit of a historical analogy. The people who built the early internet infrastructure weren't necessarily the ones who built the applications on top of it. Pre-training is becoming more like infrastructure. Open models are getting very strong, and the gap between open and closed is compressing on the base capabilities. That means a smaller, focused team can take a strong open base and pour all of their effort into the thing the big labs are structurally bad at, which is going deep on one domain.

The big labs have to be generalists. They're serving hundreds of millions of users across every possible use case, and coding is one line item among many. We can wake up every day and only think about what it takes to make an autonomous coding agent that actually works end to end. That means building the environments where the agent writes code, runs tests, reads the results, and learns from that signal at scale. It means getting really serious about long-horizon tasks, where the agent has to hold a plan in its head over hundreds of steps, which is a very different problem than answering a single prompt well.

And then the other thing I'd say is that the feedback loop with real users is a huge advantage for a startup. If you're in a developer's workflow, you learn very quickly where the model breaks, and you can fold that back into training in a way that's hard to do when you're one team inside a very large organization with a lot of competing priorities.

So I don't think of it as competing with the labs on their terms. It's picking the layer of the stack where focus beats scale, and betting that the RL and agentic layer is where the real differentiation in coding is going to come from over the next few years. I feel pretty good about that bet.

r001.rationale: It says a smaller, focused team can go deep on one domain and contrasts this with large labs’ broad responsibilities.

r002.rationale: It identifies iteration speed and fast feedback from users as advantages a startup can use to improve its chosen objective.

r003.rationale: It says big labs must serve many users and use cases, leaving coding as one line item among many competing priorities.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is, where does the advantage actually come from? If your strategy is to pre-train the same kind of model as a frontier lab, but with a fraction of the budget, that’s a very difficult position. But a coding product is more than the underlying model. It needs to understand a codebase, use tools, run tests, and iterate until the change actually works.

Coding is interesting because you can get feedback from the environment. You can execute the code. You can check whether a test passes. That gives you a way to improve the system around a particular task without having to recreate all of the knowledge acquired during pre-training.

So I’d focus on a workflow where you can build a really strong feedback loop: attempt the task, measure the outcome, learn from the failures. You can start with a capable base model and build something substantially more useful for that workflow.

The incumbents can do that too, of course. Specialization alone isn’t a moat. The question is whether you can learn faster in the particular domain you’re serving—and whether each improvement makes the product useful enough that people keep using it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends focusing on a particular coding workflow and domain, presenting that specialization as a way to build a more useful product than a startup trying to match frontier labs’ general models.

r002.rationale: It says a startup may learn faster in the particular domain it serves, using feedback from task attempts, tests, and failures.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts coding products with pre-training the same kind of model, but does not describe incumbents spreading effort thin across evaluations to pursue generality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: where does the advantage actually come from? If your strategy is to pre-train the same kind of model as the frontier labs, but with a fraction of the compute, that’s a very difficult position. You need a different axis on which to compete.

For coding, that can be the environment and the reinforcement learning loop. Writing software isn’t just predicting the next token. You make a change, run a test, inspect an error, and revise your approach. A lot of the value comes from getting that whole process to work reliably over longer tasks.

So you can start with a strong existing model and focus your resources on teaching it to operate in that setting. The hard part becomes constructing useful tasks, providing good feedback, and turning failures into improvements. If you have a better loop there, you can potentially get much better performance on a particular kind of work without having the best base model in the world.

Now, the incumbent labs can do that too. So specialization alone isn’t a moat. You have to move faster, understand the workflow more deeply, and make sure that using your product generates information that actually improves it. That’s the opportunity I’d be looking for.

r001.rationale: The response says a startup can focus resources on coding workflows and achieve much better performance on a particular kind of work without having the best base model.

r002.rationale: It explicitly identifies moving faster as part of how a startup can compete with incumbent labs.

r003.rationale: It does not describe incumbent labs spreading effort thinly across evaluations in pursuit of generality.
